ratings.excerpt: There are more twists than a bent corkscrew. … More than 30 years on, it still offers an elegant construct with a juicy star role, even if Mr Levin's endlessly self-referential tone begins to pall after a while. … Although Russell Beale makes no concessions to an American accent, he deploys his innate comic gifts with great skill.. It's a pleasure to watch his hair-trigger timing, even if he lacks the manic zest John Wood gave the role on Broadway.THE PLAY: … arthritic contrivances … Russell Beale is excellent value and there are genuinely frightening moments, but I'm not convinced this is a classic thriller.

I love thrillers but they are the devil to review because of the entirely justified convention that one mustn't give too much away. … The piece is stronger on style and jokes than dramatic substance. … Levin is almost overgenerous with the twists in his serpentine plot, and there were two startling moments that made the woman sitting next to me scream out loud. … Matthew Warchus directs a production that deftly catches both the piece's humour and its sudden thrills, with a terrific design by Rob Howell of Bruhl's sumptuous converted barn of a study adorned with the many lethal weapons he collects. … Simon Russell Beale is in splendidly baleful, blackly comic mode as the blocked author… Jonathan Groff makes a fresh-faced, apparently likeable adversary, but the other characters are thi

A series of boldly theatrical and frankly camp moments, sometimes very silly yet perfectly calculated to jolt audiences out of their seats. … The comedy thriller is not exactly staple West End fare these days but Matthew Warchus's enjoyable revival of Ira Levin's 1978 play Deathtrap suggests that the genre still has legs. … A superb performance from Simon Russell Beale… Clifford Anderson, played with genial charm by Glee star Jonathan Groff… Claire Skinner is suitably fussy and awkward as Myra… Estelle Parsons fails to convince as the Bruhls' clairvoyant neighbour. … Levin's extravagantly plotted script is full of ingenious self-reference. It is wittily self-referential, artfully made, masterly in misdirection (oh, so THAT's the victim – or is it? Which corpse is actually dead?). … Russell Beale is too good, too subtle, too profoundly human an actor to fit into a killer-thriller, however knowingly self-mocking… A fine comedy cameo from Estelle Parsons as Helga the psychic. … There are moments, in a seriously enjoyable evening, when Bruhl [Russell-Beale] gives us shards of real feeling, real ambiguous self-disgust and humanity, and makes us stop wondering who will be clobbered next, and pause to consider the pain of an old man of the theatre. … [Warchus] brings his astonishing fresh eye and constantly-surprising instincts and inventiveness to that big seventies hit – Deathtrap.
